abstract_text: The Top Predator laboratory of Morris Kahn Marine Research Station has been running a shark-tagging project in the last 4 years, as part of a long-term ecological research programme. The study takes place at an anthropogenic, seasonal aggregation area of sharks in the warm discharge waters of power plants along the Mediterranean coast of Israel. Following the tagging protocol of Sharklab (Bimini, Bahamas), 51 sharks have been tagged thus far, of which 35 were dusky sharks (Carcharhimus obscurus; 34 females and 1 male) and 16 sandbar sharks (Carcharhinus plumbeus; all male). These species are listed by the IUCN as data deficient (DD) and endangered (EN) in the Mediterranean Sea, respectively. The tagging procedure includes morphometric measurements as well as DNA, stable isotopes, blood chemistry and microbiome sampling. All tagged sharks are issued a subcutaneous PIT tag as well as a spaghetti tag. 19 dusky sharks and 10 sandbar sharks were tagged with acoustic transmitters and an array of 11 receivers was placed within the tagging site and in other aggregation areas, such as offshore mariculture facilities, throughout Israel's marine space. Results indicate thermo-regulated fidelity at human-altered habitats and size as well as sex-dependent aggregating behaviour. In the Mediterranean Sea, where shark populations have declined dramatically over the last 70 years, Israeli waters have become an oasis for coastal sharks and a hub for their research, supported by ground-breaking conservation, legislation and enforcement.

abstract_text: Acoustic telemetry is a well-established tool that has been used around the world for more than three decades to get an understanding of the spatio-temporal movements and associated behaviour of a wide range of aquatic animals. New emerging technologies are being developed continuously that allow for new research applications and designs. Examples for these new technologies are (1) real-time observations of both aquatic animals as well as their aquatic environment and (2) acoustic data storage tags. Applied real-time systems may consist of various underwater sensors, acoustic telemetry tags on aquatic animals, a surface hub that receives data from the sensors as well as from the tags, and a cloud-centric database. Such systems are now in use at several global installations. Data access is available via a mobile phone or laptop that provide real-time notifications when tagged animals are near receivers or the current state of environmental variables. Acoustic data storage tags might be used especially for far-ranging animals such as sharks and rays that might inhabit coastal and pelagic regions at different times of the year. These applications can be used to get a bigger picture of a species behaviour and its spatio-temporal distribution in order to address conservation and management measures since data is also collected while animals are outside of acoustic arrays. Here, we will explore the evolution of the use of acoustic telemetry and how receiving data in real-time and in acoustic data storage applications will help sustain our ocean ecosystems.

abstract_text: Information like habitat preferences and trophic ecology regarding juvenile white sharks Carcharodon carcharias (WS) and shortfin mako sharks Isurus oxyrinchus (MS) is lacking. This study investigates the habitat use of juvenile MS and WS in the nursery area of Sebastian Vizcaino Bay (SVB) using stable isotope analysis in multiple tissues. During 2015 and 2016, we collected muscle (n=165), blood samples (n=147), red blood cells (RBC; n=62) and plasma (n=70) of young MS and muscle (n=6), RBC (=2) and plasma (n=2) of young WS. The size range for MS was 64.5-196 cm of total length (TL) and for WS it was 130-292 cm TL. Shortfin mako and white sharks had significant differences for muscle tissue in δ13C values (W = 255.5, p < 0.0001), but not in δ15N values (W = 1189.5, p = 0.08). We did not find significant differences in δ13C values (W = 228, p-value = 0.045) and δ15N values (W = 420.5, p-value = 0.8) of whole blood between shortfin mako and white sharks. In addition, sharks with similar TL of both species (MS > 102 cm TL and WS <186 cm TL) showed a similar pattern of δ15N values for whole blood, RBCs and plasma. MS and WS with similar total length (MS> 102 cm TL and WS < 186 cm TL) reflected in their tissues (muscle, blood, RBC and plasma) the regional baseline 15-N enriched isotopic signature of SVB, suggesting that SVB has a unique isotopic signature (isoscape). The similarity in isotopic niche and isotopic composition between shortfin mako and white sharks in multiple tissues reflecting large and short time periods suggest shared resource and common habitat use inside SVB throughout extended times confirming their residency in this area during their earlier life stages.

abstract_text: Whale sharks are usually observed in coastal areas throughout the highly productive tropical and subtropical regions. The Indo-Pacific sub-population is declining mainly due to fisheries catches, bycatch and vessel strikes. Accordingly, in 2016 the species was assessed as "Endangered" on the IUCN Red List. Despite conservation concerns, there are still substantial gaps in the knowledge of whale shark ecology. This study investigates the temporal variability of whale shark presence in the South Ari Atoll Marine Protected Area (S.A.MPA). Even if the area is very limited (about 42km2) it appears to be an important aggregation site for the species in the Maldives archipelago. Since 2012 the Maldives Whale Shark Research Programme (MWSRP) has been collecting data year-round within the MPA. Due to the heterogeneity of the effort among different years only data collected between 2014 and 2017 has been considered in this study. A total of 572 sharks encounters have been reported in this period. Concurrently, in situ Sea Surface Temperature (SST) has also been collected. Sightings per Unit of Effort (SPUE) was calculated based on the number of survey trips carried out per month and per year during favorable environmental conditions (e.g. wind speed not exceed 3 in the Beaufort scale and partial and total clouds covered conditions). Generalized Linear Models have been used to analyse the temporal variability of the SPUE. No significant difference has been observed in SPUE across the study period. However, taking into consideration data on a monthly-year basis, the species' occurrence presents significant differences (P-level < 0.01). Further analysis revealed that SST could be a significant covariate. The understanding offered by this study provides additional information upon which to base an appropriate management strategy in the MPA for this wide-ranging species.

abstract_text: The North Sea is known for its natural richness. Yet it is also one of most intensively exploited seas in the world, and, as a result, fish species have disappeared or populations are reduced to low numbers. There is a growing call to restore the natural richness of the North Sea but, it is often unclear what this is, because baseline studies date back 60 years at best. Elasmobranchs are an example of a group of species of which populations in the North Sea have marginalized over the past century. These includes the critically endangered angelshark Squatina squatina and common skate Dipturus intermedius. We review the historical abundance and some life-history aspects of these species in the Dutch marine waters using a variety of historical sources. Palaeontological sources dating back to the origin of the North Sea suggest that these species always have been present in the area. Written historical sources from the 16th to the 19th century suggest that the angelshark used to be fairly common and that the common skate was indeed common. Catch reports indicate that the angel shark started to decline at the onset of the 20th century and went locally extinct in the 1970s. Landings and fishery-independent data of common skate show a similar picture. The start of the decline coincides with the onset of steam-powered fisheries whereas the demise follows on the intensification of diesel-powered beam-trawlers. Historical reports and catch data indicates that angelsharks mainly visited the area in summer to reproduce. Common skates were mainly caught in winter and these were mostly young individuals that supposedly used the area as nursery grounds. Our study shows that if we base our ideas of a North Sea ecosystem on a baseline view after 1900 we may have overly low expectations of its potential natural richness.

abstract_text: The decline of elasmobranch populations in the Mediterranean Sea highlights the need of developing effective management strategies. The biological traits of such organisms include internal fertilization, hence decoupling mating from egg release/parturition, a longer life and a slower growth rate compared to most teleosts, making elasmobranch populations particularly vulnerable to fishery exploitation. Because of their biology, these species distribution may vary drastically among life stages (e.g. adults vs juveniles, pregnant vs non-pregnant females) and sexes. Movements across Mediterranean water bodies, between mating, parturitions, feeding areas and the occurrence of aggregations in a specific area are fundamental points for understanding their ecology. Therefore, integrating movement information in management strategies of these species is a crucial step forward. Such data on pelagic and benthic species are scarce throughout the Mediterranean Sea and especially in the Adriatic Sea. In this study, we adopted a conventional tagging approach in the Adriatic Sea using "spaghetti" tags in collaboration with professional and recreational fishermen, elasmobranchs, caught as target or bycatch, were tagged and released after species identification, recording size, sex and maturity (for males by clasper calcification and for females TL50 was used if known) and storing release coordinates in Tshark.org database. So far, we tagged 592 individuals (12 species) among which the majority are smooth-hound sharks (Mustelus mustelus and M. punctulatus), eagle ray (Myliobatis aquila) and pelagic sting ray (Pteroplatytrygon violacea). We received 6 recapture reports out of 301 of tagged Mustelus spp, ranging between 6 months to 5 days after release, and 1 of pelagic sting ray, after 2 months and 15 days after release. The longest distance recoded was of 20 nautical miles (NM) for Mustelus spp and 125 NM for P. violacea. As this approach relies on the recapture reporting, the collaboration between research institutions across Mediterranean countries, and between researchers and fishermen as well, is fundamental to increase recapture information.

abstract_text: Elasmobranchs constitute a target or bycatch of a wide variety of fishing techniques. Such anthropogenic pressure has brought to a drastic reduction of local populations across the Mediterranean Sea. Moreover, limited-data collection and species misidentification, among others, have led to a scarcity of historical data on species occurrence and abundance trends in several taxa. Such information is particularly valuable to study migration dynamics and behaviour variations, as well as to reconstruct historical trends. To fill this data gap, the use of local ecological knowledge from professional fishermen can be considered as a valuable source of semi-quantitative information on several aspects of species ecology, abundance and behavioural aspects. Through a questionnaire survey, fishermen operating with diverse fishing gears such as bottom and pelagic trawlers, set nets and longlines were interviewed by trained researchers with the aid of photo-identification materials. A total of 211 interviews were collected across nine Mediterranean FAO-GSA sub-areas (9, 10, 11, 16, 17, 18, 19, 22, 28). Results covered a wide range of elasmobranch species with regard to coastal, pelagic and deep-sea environment. Interviewers indicated species that were abundant in the past, declined recently and showed size variation compared to past catches. Moreover, fishermen reported aggregation sightings/events, seasonal movements and species-specific fishing area. The present study constitutes a baseline regarding abundance and distribution of elasmobranch species in historical times and may represent a valuable tool for data deficient taxa. It also gives new insights on elasmobranchs behavioural and ecological aspects and highlights priority species and suitable geographic areas for conservation and behavioural studies.

abstract_text: It is known that juveniles whale sharks (Rhincodon typus) have tendency to gather, seasonally, in a few coastal areas around the world to feed on zooplankton; however little is known about their food preferences. The CSS (Centro Studi Squali) scientific coordinator of the project "Whale shark feeding ecology" (in partnership with University of Calabria, University of Siena, ISPRA, University of Naples Federico II, Stazione Zoologica Anton Dohrn), in 2016, started the study of these aggregations. During field observations we collected zooplankton samples and we observed feeding behaviour of sharks to understand the main characteristics of the zooplankton community that appears to cause said gatherings. So far two expeditions (2017 and 2018) have been carried out in the channel of Mozambique, in the coastal waters of the Nosy Be (MG). Here whale sharks are present in the last four months of the year: data were collected in the eastern part of the island in late November-early December which is the peak season for whale shark sightings in the area. Zooplankton samples were collected vertically from 10 m depth to surface, using a net with 200 µm mesh aperture. The samples were concentrated using a 50µm filter and fixed with alcohol (70%) and lugol (1%). At the same time, location, water temperature and transparency, shark presence/absence and feeding behaviour were recorded. Quantitative and qualitative analysis of zooplankton samples were performed at Stazione Zoologica Anton Dohrn and ISPRA laboratories. We calculated zooplankton biomass and abundance. We identified at species level the most important zooplanktonic taxa (copepods, chetognats etc) and moreover we calculated their size spectra.

abstract_text: The knowledge of Hexanchus vitulus (Springer & Waller, 1969) and other deep-sea sharks in the Caribbean Sea is considered scarce, as these species are unfrequently captured by local artisanal fishers and therefore scientific research regarding its biology has not been developed. The present study reports the first record with morphometry data of H. vitulus in this area, in order to provide useful information for future comparisons of specimens in other coastal regions. A total of ten Atlantic six gill sharks was captured offshore El Quetzalito, Guatemala (15.740379 N, -88.274621W) by artisanal fishers at using longlines and fishing nets at a depth of 275-365 m. The date of capture, fishing gear, used bait, sex, total length, precaudal length, and fork length were registered from each shark. Taxonomic identification was carried out through the description published by Compagno et al., (2005) and Daly-Engel et al., (2018). All the specimens were identified as H. vitulus due to the presence of six gills, a slender body with brown dorsal and white ventral coloration, narrow head and mouth, anterior serrations on lower teeth, and large eyes. These characteristics are the same described for H. nakamurai, because H. vitulus has been describes as a cryptic species with no evident external differentiation known to date. The length of the specimens ranged between 61-165 cm TL, with a mean of 142 ± 29 SD cm TL. Most of the captured sharks were considered mature individuals with the exception of a juvenile female caught in 2015. Sex ratio of this sample was 2.3:1 (Males:Females), where 90% of the sharks were mature individuals. The high quantity of mature sharks in this sample differs from what observed in other relatively close areas like Belize. Arguments regarding a potential segregation between mature and immature individuals related to locality and month are presented.

abstract_text: The ecology of mantas and echeneids in the Eastern Tropical Pacific is poorly understood. In this study we describe the frequency of interactions between the vulnerable Mobula birostris and its symbiont Remora remora, through the participation of scientists and tourists in a marine protected area. Data were obtained by the analysis of underwater pictures of observed mantas with remoras during 139 diving days at sea during the years 2016-2017. A total of 273 records of mantas with remoras was registered from 207 identified individuals. Estimated size of mantas ranged from 250-550 cm DW, with an average size of 380 ± 50 cm SD. Sex ratio of mantas was 1.3:1 (Female:Male) as observed from our sample of 89 females (42.9%), 68 males (32.8%), and 50 individuals (24%) for which sex could not be determined. The remora species observed in all the mantas was the common remora Remora remora. Average number of remoras attached to the mantas was 1.6 ± 0.56 remoras per manta. Estimated size of the remora ranged between 40-80 cm TL, with an average of 60 cm ± 10 cm SD. During the study period, there were no significant differences between months and the number of remoras per manta (H7,271=5.13; p=0.64). Most of the mantas usually had one or two remoras, 43 % (n=117) and 53.5 % (n=147), respectively; while 2.5% of the mantas (n=5) were observed with three remoras, and only two individuals with four (0.9%). Although a higher number of remoras in female mantas was observed, there was no significant differences according to the morphotype or sex of the mantas (H3,208=7.90; p=0.04) confirmed by the Bonferroni post-hoc test. The study of this host-symbiont interaction is discussed in terms of the potential insights that this kind of research could provide regarding the ecology of mantas and remoras if compared with other aggregation sites.

abstract_text: In the years 2017, 2018 and 2019 the feeding behavior of the whale shark has been studied off Nosy Be Island (Madagascar). In particular, the investigations involved the description of the behavioral modules of the whale shark and their relationship with the phytoplankton communities. In total, 65 phytoplankton samples were collected in the following four behavioural conditions: 0 - absence of whale sharks; 1 - presence of swimming whale sharks; 2 - presence of whale sharks in horizontal feeding; 3 - presence of whale sharks in vertical passive feeding; 4 - presence of whale sharks in vertical active feeding. All samples were immediately filtered and then frozen to be subsequently analyzed by HPLC to identify the total biomass and contribution of the different functional groups of phytoplankton. In total 8 phytoplanctonic taxa have been identified: Prasinophyceae, Dinoflagellata, Cryptophyceae, Primnesiophyceae, Pelagophyceae, Chlorophyceae, Cyanobacteria and Bacillariophyceae. Among them, Cryptophyceae were the most abundant. Our results seemed to highlight a certain correlation also between behavioral feeding intensity exhibited by sharks and the total biomass of phytoplancton. In particular, this appeared more evident with some groups of algae that might be involved in the release of the dimethyl sulfonio propionate (DMSP). This substance is produced by algal organisms in response to predation by zooplankton organisms. Since DMSP is a substance characterized by a strong odor, the results could demonstrate the fundamental role of smell in the identification of food sources by the whale shark, as confirmed for marine birds.

abstract_text: Despite in recent years the interest about the human-made noise effects on marine animals have received notably increasing, at date few studies have investigated the potential role of acoustic masking on animal's bio-ecological relationship. In this study, we exposed twelve specimens of small-spotted catshark (Scyliorhinus canicula, Linnaeus 1758) to biological and anthropogenic sounds in order to assess their behavioural changes potentially referable to pray presence and masking effect due to the shipping noise. Specifically, the sharks held individually in aquarium were exposed to three acoustic experimental conditions differentiated in their spectral (Hz) components (biological and anthropogenic mixed sources) and intensity (dB re 1 µPa) levels. abstract_text: Marine heatwaves (MHWs) are known to have large-scale implications over entire ecosystems, however, their effects over key predators, such as elasmobranchs, are still poorly understood. Although multiples studies have revealed several developmental, physiological, and behavioural implications of temperature increase in this group, this has yet to be addressed in an MHW context. While no changes were observed in food intake, cue response, and foraging time, there was an increase in the number of turns and biting events. As anthropogenic climate change continues unabated, MHWs are expected to increase in frequency, duration and intensity, which may further challenge the foraging efficiency of these key predators, with potential cascading consequences in ecosystems already subjected increasing pressure.

abstract_text: White sharks are usually defined as generalist predators, with a well described ontogenetic dietary shift that occurs between the subadult and adult stages. Yet the majority of published studies have focused on large and mature individuals, so the information about feeding habits is still lacking for young white sharks. It is imperative to improve information about the trophic ecology of white sharks across life-stages to better understand habitat shifts and their early life movements inside nursery areas, which are determined by resources availability. This study provides the first insight into the trophic ecology of young white sharks using stable isotopes analysis (SIA) in muscle tissues to characterize prey contributions and ontogenetic changes in habitat use. White shark isotopic values did not vary by sex (δ15N values: W = 52, p = 0.8 and δ13C values: t = 0.25, p = 0.8) as well as age classes (δ15N values: W =54, p = 0.4 and δ13C values: t = -0.9, p = 0.4) and we did not find variation based on size classes for δ13C and δ15N. However, we found changes in prey composition across white shark life stages, with significant changes throughout ontogeny. Mixing model indicate a high use of coastal areas for foraging, which likely represents the shift from the embryo's typical maternally-derived isotopic signature incorporated in offshore foraging regions to the postpartum isotopic composition, incorporated by neonates from inshore nursery habitats, including SVB. This study reinforces the assertion that coastal areas, like SVB and the prey preferences that take place in this area (from previous research) are critical for the development and to the successful foraging of young white sharks, providing relevant knowledge regarding this species.

abstract_text: Elasmobranchs are among the most successful vertebrates in the Phanerozoic, with a stratigraphic distribution ranging from the Silurian to Recent times and a global distribution. Like other vertebrates, they share the use of bioapatite in making mineralized tissues. Bioapatite represents a unique archive of physical and chemical environmental information. Indeed, bioapatite lattice can accommodate iso- and hetero-valent substitutions during life or after burial and diagenesis, with a variation of the chemical composition during geological time. Chemical and crystal-chemical data can be achieved by different analytical tools, like laser ablation inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (LA-ICPMS). As LA-ICPMS results are affected by physical-chemical preperties of the sample matrix, an internal standard is usually required to correct and validate the analytical results. Unluckily, an exclusive internal standard is so far missing for bioapatite, strongly affected by isomorphic sobstitutions. A possible solution can be the calibration with external standards which, however, are not so diffused. We propose herein a new method to prepare home-made matrix-matched calibration standards to measure major element concentrations. The method has been tested on living and fossil shark teeth. The final goal is the development of a reliable tool for chemical characterization by LA-ICPMS on small sized samples, avoiding the use of electron microprobe, that is considered a more appropriate technique, but which is more expensive, less diffused and, in any case, once again strictly dependent on the calibrating standards. Our technique can be useful to study teeth of living elasmobranchs in order to find possible chemical and crystal-chemical variation in bioapatite related, for example, to specific habitat, age, gender, etc.

abstract_text: Anthropogenic derived contamination is a daily threat to marine resources. Long-living and slow growing, higher trophic level animals like sharks are usually the most affected. However, positive correlations were found between skin and muscle metal levels, across all tested elements. Transparent and white colours resulted the debris with the highest frequency of ingestion (O%= 25). Fragments were the most common litter in stomachs of both S. canicula (O%= 87.5%) and R. clavata (O%= 75), whereas in G. melastomus fragments and filaments occurred with the same frequency (O%= 50). Most litter particles (55.5% of total debris) had a size less than 5 mm. This is the first time that litter ingestion is observed in R. clavata in Mediterranean waters. Some of these species could be considered as indicators for litter ingestion in marine demersal habitats.

abstract_text: Increasing interest in the management and conservation of elasmobranchs highlights the importance of acquiring further knowledge of their biology and ecology; in this respect, important information can be derived from the analysis of their parasite fauna. Parasitological investigations focused on elasmobranchs from Mediterranean Sea are scarce; the compilation of accurate and updated checklists is further complicated by the occurrence of old records of infection and the doubtful identity of the shark host. A healthy specimen of Common Smoothhound, Mustelus mustelus, (total length: 66 cm) fished as bycatch in northern Adriatic Sea was subjected to a complete parasitological examination. Collected parasites were processed for morphological and morphometric analyses aimed at identifying them to the species level. Parasite identity was confirmed through amplification and sequencing of 28S rDNA. Nematodes belonging to the species Acanthocheilus rotundatus (15 specimens) were recovered from the stomach and the proximal intestine, while cestodes belonging to the species Calliobothrium verticillatum (5 specimens) were collected from the spiral valve. Calliobothrium spp. are known to parasitize different species of Mustelus around the world's oceans. Particularly, C. verticillatum has been reported in M. mustelus from Northeastern Atlantic and only one report dating back to the 50s on this parasite in M. mustelus from Mediterranean Sea exists. Our results would therefore confirm the occurrence of this host-parasite association in Mediterranean waters. Acanthocheilus rotundatus has been described infecting M. mustelus from Adriatic Sea based on morphological evidence; our work provides the first sequence data of A. rotundatus from Mediterranean Sea, since only sequences of specimens collected in extra-Mediterranean areas were available so far. Updated knowledge on the parasite fauna of M. mustelus from Adriatic Sea would contribute to elucidate aspects of the ecology, biology and health status of elasmobranchs from Mediterranean Sea, providing useful information for their proper management and conservation.

abstract_text: The advent of Next Generation Sequencing (NGS) technologies has seen a transition from conservation genetics to genomics (from gene to genome scales), which is informing our understanding of species and improving conservation outcomes based on these insights. This technology has provided access to thousands of genome-wide markers, collectively capable of providing reliable inferences about demographic patterns and enabling detection of local adaptation. Examples of applied genomics in elasmobranch conservation and forensics at different levels, from species to individuals are becoming more common as we develop genomic resources for non-model species. For species identification, when diagnostic external morphological characters are lacking, or when identifications rely on body parts, the use of non-expensive techniques such as mtDNA sequencing is often used. However, when dealing with closely related, recently diverged species, as is the case of the Galapagos (Carcharhinus galapagensis) and dusky (C. obscurus) sharks, the combination of mtDNA and genome-wide diagnostic markers is required to distinguish the species. This also allows other biologically relevant patterns of genetic variation to be explored, such as those that arise due to hybridization. A first population connectivity assessment of C. galapagensis in the Eastern Tropical Pacific resulted in the development of 1,873 high-resolution SNP markers. A selected subset of SNPs was further used to successfully assess hybridisation patterns between this, and C. obscurus. Future steps include the use of such markers as forensic tools to develop a cost-effective PCR-based essay to rapidly distinguish the two species from carcases or body parts. Likewise, the development of worldwide genomic resources capable of detecting population structure at large as well as fine geographic scales is crucial at the population level to identify particular signatures of selection and local adaptation that can lead to provenience-detecting markers. Finally, at the individual level the inference of the sex-determination systems in new species is leading the way towards the identification of sex-linked markers that can aid sex identification from fin or tissue samples. Current efforts using in silico and PCR validations are showing that SNP markers can be effective at assigning the correct sex in at least twelve of the sixteen species tested. Applying fundamental knowledge towards the development of molecular traceability tools is the logical and much needed step towards shark conservation.

abstract_text: In the Mediterranean Sea, sharks are currently one of the less frequently observed groups of animals. Scientific surveys do not provide enough observation effort to collect relevant data on the presence and distribution of the species, and fisheries data have been historically scattered and rarely adequate in terms of taxonomic resolution. Following the IUCN regional assessment 57% of the species are listed as endangered and 25 % as still data deficient. New monitoring strategies need to take place in the area to improve data collection, and new technologies can create a link between people and scientists. Data management is crucial in these cases. Here we present sharkPulse, a collaborative international project aiming to involve divers, fishermen, surfers, beachgoers and other ocean users in sharing image-based sightings of sharks. To facilitate users participation the sharkPulse team has developed a web platform (http:\\sharkpulse.org) and a mobile application (IOS and Android). All the data collected are available and shared online with summary tables and distribution maps. To break linguistic barriers and boost participation, the project has created national focal points in several parts of the world (Italy, UK, New Zealand, South Africa, Greece). From 2016, the Italian national focal point has focused his activity on the Mediterranean Sea, collecting more than 900 photographic records of 35 shark species. Here we present a first exploration of these data and highlight some emerging patterns: i) possible identification of strongholds for rare and endangered species; ii) seasonal shifts in pelagic shark distributions; and iii) presence of newborns and immature specimens for broad-ranging species such as the shortfin mako (Isurus oxyrinchus) for which these sightings are more frequent (75% of the records) than adults. Integrated collection and analysis of these data can improve scientific understanding of sharks in the Mediterranean Sea, fill the data gap that has historically characterized the basin on these species, and stimulate conservation and recovery actions.

title: Shark and Ray Forensics, a conservation tool for the Western Indian Ocean region

abstract_text: Worldwide, ocean and coastal threat is driven by the rapid expansion of fisheries and global trade markets, whereby overfishing activities and habitat degradation have severely altered elasmobranch populations. The western Indian Ocean is an important conservation area for sharks and rays as this region is a global hotspot for biodiversity and for threatened species. The harvesting of elasmobranchs in this region is amongst others driven by the international shark meat and shark fin trade. In this study, we assessed marine forensics as a tool for complementing traditional identification methods – through the development of a mini-barcoding assay as well as High Resolution Melt (HRM) analysis, relevant to elasmobranch species occurring in the western Indian Ocean region. This involved the testing and optimisation of the standard barcoding region of the cytochrome oxidase c subunit 1 (COI), using traditional barcoding primers as well as two sets of nested PCR primers in a multiplex assay. Preliminary results (only a 22% species identification success rate) indicated the limitations of using only the traditional COI primers and warrented the inclusion of additional gene regions for species identification of future shark forensic cases. In this study, a mini-barcoding multiplex assay comprising three primer sets were optimised and applied to a wide range of shark forensic case studies, involving confiscated shark fins possibly for illegal trade. Furthermore, a HRM approach was validated based on six southern African houndshark species and further optimised for additional commercially exploited species such as hammerhead S. lewini and S. zygaena, copper C. brachyurus, dusky C. obscurus, bull C. leucas, blacktip C. limbatus and blue shark P. glauca. Ultimately, these approaches can be combined to develop a relatively fast and cost-effective identification protocol that can be applied to identify most, if not all, elasmobranch species involved in trade regionally.

abstract_text: Over-exploitation and fishery by-catch leads to an increasing decline of elasmobranchs worlwide; with unpredictable consequences for the health and structure of the ecosystems. According to IUCN, the Mediterranean Sea is amongst the three top regions where the biodiversity of sharks and rays is seriously threatened. Considering the European waters, the IUCN reveals that half of the assessed elasmobranch species, 39 out of 73, are threatened at Mediterranean level. Despite some recent efforts in EU to reduce shark by-catch and mortality (i.e., adoption of the European Commission's Action plan for the Conservation and Management of Sharks, and adoption of the Council Regulation (EU) 2017/127), the EC goals are far from being achieved, and conservation actions need to be set up. Current legislation only prevents retention and trade, but not the actual capture or the mortality that may occur as a result. The factors that contribute to the by-catch and the mortality of elasmobranch during fisheries capture are - in fact - many, but the major is the fishers' attitude. The consciuous and responsible behavior of the employees in commercial fishing activities is fundamental to mitigate the impact of their actions on the marine biodiversity, cartilaginous fishes included. The project eLIFE (elasmobranch low impact fishing experience), has been recently funded by the EU's LIFE programme for the protection of the enviornment. It aims to reduce the elasmobranch by-catch and mortality by promoting best conservation practices in the context of the EU commercial fishing activities in the Mediterranean Sea. It targets several sharks listed as endengered or critically endengered in the Red List of the European marine fishes of the IUCN and it includes the partecipation of 3 EU countries (Italy, Cyprus and Greece). eLIFE is based on the direct involvement of the professional fishers, and will test the efficiency of using low impact fishing gears and correct methods of manipulation for the elasmobranch incidental caught, as well as the use of digital technology, like satellite tags and a smartphone application to monitor the efficency of the conservation actions and to obtain new spatial information.

abstract_text: The Angelshark (Squatina squatina) was once widespread throughout the Eastern Atlantic and Mediterranean Sea, but now is one of the most threatened fish in European waters. Indeed, the angel shark family is identified as the second most threatened elasmobranch taxon after a global review of extinction risk by the IUCN. A unique stronghold remains for the Angelshark in the Canary Islands, but even here the species is under threat. Given the importance of forging bonds with key stakeholders to secure the future of this species, Angel Shark Project: Canary Islands (ASP:CI), a collaboration between Universidad de Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, Zoological Society of London and Zoologisches Forschungsmuseum Alexander Koenig, has developed a number of tools to engage interested parties and encourage them to provide information to aid scientific research. Our focus is on the recreational sector, specifically divers and fishers. This year, ASP:CI has re-launched best practice guidelines in collaboration with the recreational fishing sector to a) encourage fishers to safely release any accidentally caught Angelsharks, b) report these encounters and c) gain the trust of the fishing community and raise the awareness on the species. In addition, we completed the first Count the Angels event in Fuerteventura, which brings together dive centres to complete a census of Angelsharks across the island via coordinated diving. A total of 7 dive centres participated, 24 Angelsharks sighted and over 882 diving hours were completed during this event. This not only reinforces the bond with the diving community, but enables greater coverage across large stretches of coastline to better understand Angelshark presence, and in the future, calculate abundance metrics. These tools will ensure and reinforce the bond between scientists and the recreational community, a key task when working with a Critically Endangered species.

abstract_text: Marine megafauna (elasmobranchs, mammals, turtles, birds) is important from an ecological point of view because it occupies upper trophic levels and is also often essential for marine tourism. Species belonging to this group are often heavily impacted by fishing due to their longevity, late sexual maturity and low reproductive output, which affect the capability to recover from depletion. In the Galapagos, marine megafauna is protected throughout the marine reserve and is the main attraction for marine tourism, generating millions of dollars in revenue annually. Multiple artisanal longlining projects were carried out since the 1990s with the aim of redirecting fishing effort from the depleted coastal-demersal species to pelagic fish, such as yellowfin tuna, Thunnus albacares and swordfish, Xiphias gladius. All these projects have resulted in high bycatch of megafauna. Despite its importance in the archipelago, megafauna is still being caught as bycatch in the longline fishery, without independent scientific studies to evaluate its impact, largely due to poor objective definition, data collection, and enforcement. To fill in this knowledge gap, we analyzed data of the fifth longline fishing project (2012-2013) to describe the fishery, identify variables affecting bycatch, and suggest mitigation strategies. This experimental project involved twelve fishing vessels, which deployed 42,007 hooks catching 4,893 individuals belonging to 33 species, mostly yellowfin tuna. Of those, 16 species were protected megafauna, particularly blacktip sharks, Carcharhinus limbatus and oceanic manta, Manta birostris. These species were regularly captured during the two fishing seasons and in all the four bioregions that occur in the archipelago, suggesting little potential to mitigate their catch. As an alternative, we identified 14 hotspots where yellowfin tuna and swordfish could be harvested through more selective fishing techniques. In an archipelago where the main economic activity is marine wildlife tourism, the implementation of an extractive and unselective activity such as pelagic longline fishing should be avoided to ensure the preservation of the Galapagos marine ecosystem and its booming tourism industry.

abstract_text: Fishers have a rich knowledge of the resources and the environment in which they work, that is rarely utilised to provide advice on the status of exploited populations. Fishers "local ecological knowledge" (LEK) can be used to reconstruct species trends, like sharks, that currently are at very low biomass due to overfishing. In this study we used the historical memories of Sicilian fishers to gather data on change in fishing practices and capture of cartilaginous species in the Strait of Sicily over the last decades. We conducted interviews with 27 retired trawl fishers from Mazara del Vallo harbour (SW Sicily) using a pre-defined questionnaire with a series of open and fixed questions and comparing to the present abundance. The questionnaire included specific questions about the trends they perceived in cartilaginous fish occurence abundance between 1940s and 2000s (according to three main time periods 1940-1960, 1961-1980 and 1981-2010), in order to facilitate the estimation of eventual changes over time. A total of 29 species were mentioned by fishermen during interviews, including large pelagic sharks (Carcharhinidae, Sphyrnidae and Lamnidae), mesopredatory demersal sharks (Squalidae, Hexanchidae, Centrophoridae, Oxynotidae, Triakidae, Scyliorhinidae and Squatinidae) and batoids. Overall shark catches were perceived to have diminished since the early 1940s: about 95% of fishers reported the decline of commercially important species (e.g. Mustelus spp.) and indicated species that could have been depleted (e.g. Squatina spp., Sphyrna spp.). Our study shows that LEK of fishers can be beneficial for reconstructing long-term population trends of exploited species when traditional standard data on fisheries catch or species relative abundance from surveys is limited or only available for recent periods. The results obtained cleary indicate the rapid and alarming decline of elasmobranchs in the Strait of Sicily highlighting the need for urgent conservation measures to be adopted.
